Webshare is cheaper if your usage is steady: 10 GB costs $27.50 against roughly $35 at ProxyEmpire's entry rate, 100 GB costs $225, its 80M+ pool is larger, and the free datacenter tier is handy for testing. ProxyEmpire is the better choice when usage swings month to month, because nothing you prepay is lost, and when you need mobile proxies, ISP-level targeting or a combined residential and mobile trial. For predictable monthly scraping, pick Webshare; for bursty work or account management, pick ProxyEmpire.

Webshare and ProxyEmpire both target cost-conscious buyers, but they treat unused bandwidth in opposite ways. Webshare sells cheap monthly residential allowances that reset every 30 days. ProxyEmpire sells prepaid traffic that rolls over indefinitely. Webshare also has a larger advertised pool, a free datacenter plan and a polished API; ProxyEmpire adds mobile proxies and free ISP targeting. This comparison helps you work out which model costs less for the way you actually use proxies.

blocks.text: Webshare in 2026: what you get

Webshare is the self-service favourite of solo developers. It gives away 10 shared datacenter proxies with 1 GB a month forever, sells paid datacenter lists from $2.99 for 100 proxies, and offers static ISP and rotating residential networks with a clean dashboard and good API. Its rotating residential pool is listed at 80M+ IPs in 195 countries, with sticky sessions from one minute to 24 hours. The main catch is that monthly bandwidth resets every 30 days and does not roll over.

Strengths: Permanent free datacenter plan for testing; Low, transparent residential pricing; Excellent dashboard and API; Sticky sessions up to 24 hours. Weak spots: Bandwidth resets monthly with no rollover; No mobile proxies; 500-request default concurrency limit.
ProxyEmpire in 2026: what you get

ProxyEmpire is a Bulgarian-registered provider (SWIFT SAAS LTD) that has been selling since 2020. Its residential and mobile networks share one system with 30M+ advertised IPs in 170+ countries, and country, region, city and ISP targeting are included at no extra cost. The standout policy is bandwidth rollover: prepaid traffic carries forward indefinitely, even after a subscription lapses. Proxyway's 2026 market tests found ProxyEmpire's pool was the third largest among the providers it tested.

Strengths: Prepaid traffic rolls over indefinitely; ISP/ASN targeting included at no extra cost; Cheap $1.97 trial covering residential and mobile; Unlimited residential option priced per day. Weak spots: Smaller advertised pool than the big three; Exact GB thresholds for each tier only shown at checkout; Weaker results on Google in some independent tests.
Pricing: Webshare vs ProxyEmpire

Webshare's rotating residential plans cost $3.50 for 1 GB, $27.50 for 10 GB, $65 for 25 GB, $225 for 100 GB and $875 for 500 GB per month, falling to $1.40/GB at 3 TB. Yearly billing is about 30% cheaper but is paid upfront for a 360-day term. Unused bandwidth resets every 30 days.

ProxyEmpire's rotating residential pricing currently starts at $3.50/GB (shown as 50% off a $7 list price) and steps down through several tiers to $1.50/GB at 1 TB, with custom pricing from about $0.75/GB above 5 TB. Rotating mobile starts at $4.50/GB, rotating datacenter at about $0.65/GB, and a flat-rate unlimited residential plan is sold by the day.

At 10 GB a month, Webshare is the cheaper option at about $27.50 against $35 for ProxyEmpire, roughly 21% less. At 100 GB, a like-for-like total is harder to state because ProxyEmpire does not publish an exact price for that volume; Webshare comes to about $225. Look past the per-GB figure too. ProxyEmpire lets unused traffic carry forward, while Webshare's allowance does not (allowance resets every 30 days; no rollover). For irregular workloads, that difference can outweigh a small gap in list price.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

By advertised size, Webshare (80M+) is about 2.7x larger than ProxyEmpire (30M+). Advertised pool sizes are marketing figures counted over long periods; the number of IPs actually reachable in a given country at a given moment is far smaller for every provider, so treat these as a rough guide to depth rather than a guarantee. For coverage, Webshare lists 195 countries and ProxyEmpire lists 170+. On targeting, Webshare offers country, plus state, city or ZIP (US) or ASN, while ProxyEmpire offers country, region, city and ISP/ASN (included by default).
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, Webshare offers rotating or sticky from 1 minute to 24 hours, and ProxyEmpire offers rotating or sticky sessions up to 24 hours. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. Webshare: low prices and a developer-friendly API. ProxyEmpire: stable connections and traffic that never expires. Let price and the countries you need decide.

SERP and rank tracking: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. Webshare: fine for light rank tracking. ProxyEmpire: Google was its weakest target in independent tests. Let price and the countries you need decide.

Social media and multi-account management: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Webshare: 24-hour sticky sessions and cheap static ISP IPs. With ProxyEmpire: residential and mobile IPs with 24-hour sticky sessions. Run the same small test on both before committing.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: ProxyEmpire. ProxyEmpire has the edge here. Why: free city and ISP targeting. How Webshare compares: good for US work with ZIP targeting, thinner elsewhere.

Ad verification and geo-testing: ProxyEmpire wins. The deciding factor for ProxyEmpire: ISP-level targeting at no extra cost. The limitation on the Webshare side: no mobile network and limited selector combinations.
Tight budgets: Webshare. Webshare has the edge here. Why: free tier plus some of the lowest per-GB rates here. How ProxyEmpire compares: rollover means nothing you pay for is wasted.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Webshare: 10 free datacenter proxies (1 GB/month); no residential trial. ProxyEmpire: $1.97 trial with 100 MB residential and 50 MB mobile. Verification and payment rules differ too. Webshare: ID checks only when flagged or for restricted categories. ProxyEmpire: Standard verification. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Webshare and ProxyEmpire before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle Webshare vs ProxyEmpire faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Webshare: 10 free datacenter proxies (1 GB/month); no residential trial; ProxyEmpire: $1.97 trial with 100 MB residential and 50 MB mobile).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.

3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country. 4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Webshare comes out ahead in 1, ProxyEmpire in 2, and 3 are ties. That makes ProxyEmpire the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Webshare is strongest for solo developers and small teams, while ProxyEmpire is strongest for teams that hate losing unused bandwidth. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
